title: The ENTIRE History of Russia in 10 Minutes
youtube_title: The ENTIRE History of Russia in 10 Minutes (862–1991)
description:
From Vikings to the space race, this is the whole story of Russia from 862 to 1991 in about ten minutes: Rurik and the Rus, Vladimir's choice of religion, the Mongols, Ivan the Terrible, Peter the Great and his beard tax, Catherine the Great, the sale of Alaska, the Russian Revolution, the Soviet Union, Gagarin and the end of the USSR. Every fact is checked.

Chapters are added automatically.

#history #russia #russianhistory #peterthegreat #animatedhistory

beats.say: April 12th, 1961. A twenty-seven-year-old Soviet pilot named Yuri Gagarin is strapped on top of a giant rocket.
As the engines roared, he said one famous word: Poyekhali! Let's go!
He circled the whole Earth once, in about an hour and forty-eight minutes. He was the first human in space.
Then he parachuted into a farm field, where a woman and her granddaughter stared at the stranger in a bright orange suit.
Have you... come from outer space?
As a matter of fact, I have!
So how did a land of forests, farmers and tsars end up in space? For that, we have to go back eleven hundred years.

show.text: The ENTIRE History of Russia in 10 Minutes
show.sub: From Vikings to the Soviet Union, 862 to 1991

beats.say: In the 800s there was no Russia. Slavic and Finnish tribes lived in the forests along big rivers.
Across the Baltic Sea lived the Vikings, Norse traders and raiders who rowed their ships deep into those rivers.
Here's the twist. Russia's oldest history book says the tribes kept fighting each other, so they invited the Vikings to rule them.
The chronicle has them say: our land is great and rich, but there is no order in it. Come and rule over us.

show.text: Our land is great and rich, but there is no order in it. Come to rule and reign over us.
show.who: The Russian Primary Chronicle, written around 1113 (Cross translation)

beats.say: Wait. You're inviting Vikings? On purpose?
We tried running it ourselves. It got messy.
That skit is our joke. The chronicle says a Viking named Rurik came in 862 and ruled from Novgorod, but historians aren't even sure he existed.
These Vikings were called the Rus. That's where the name Russia comes from.
Soon the Rus moved their capital south to Kyiv, a rich trading city. Their state is called Kyivan Rus.
Around 988, Prince Vladimir of Kyiv wanted one religion for his people. The chronicle says he went shopping.
Islam, my prince? Wonderful faith. But no alcohol.
Drinking is the joy of the Rus. Next!
That line really is in the chronicle. His envoys were dazzled by Hagia Sophia, the giant church in Constantinople, so he chose that city's Orthodox Christianity.
Historians think politics mattered too: the deal let Vladimir marry Anna, the sister of the emperor in Constantinople.
In 1237, a terrifying army rode in from the east: the Mongols, led by Batu Khan, a grandson of Genghis Khan.
In December 1240 they captured Kyiv. Most Rus princes had to pay tribute, basically protection money, to the Mongol kingdom called the Golden Horde.
Princes even had to travel to the Mongol court for permission to rule. Imagine asking the bully for a hall pass.
Meanwhile, a small town called Moscow got very good at collecting that tribute, and grew rich and strong.
In 1380 Moscow's prince even beat a Golden Horde army at Kulikovo. The Horde struck back and burned Moscow two years later.
In 1480, Moscow's army faced the Horde's army across the Ugra River. After weeks of staring, the Horde army just went home.
And that was the end of Mongol rule over Moscow.

show.label: Rus princes paid tribute to the Mongols for about

beats.say: In 1547, a sixteen-year-old named Ivan was crowned with a brand-new title: tsar, meaning emperor, from the Roman word Caesar.

tag.text: Ivan IV, the first crowned tsar

beats.say: We call him Ivan the Terrible. In Russian it's closer to Ivan the Fearsome.
He grew the country fast, and in Moscow he had Saint Basil's Cathedral built, with its famous onion domes.
Legend says Ivan then blinded the architects so they could never build anything as beautiful. It's a myth: the builder kept working for years afterward.
But he was also cruel and paranoid. His private army terrorized his own people, and in 1581, by most accounts, he killed his eldest son in a fit of rage.
With no strong heir, Russia fell into chaos called the Time of Troubles: fake heirs, famine, and even a Polish army in Moscow.
In 1613, an assembly picked a sixteen-year-old noble, Michael Romanov, as tsar. His family would rule for over three hundred years.
In 1682, a nine-year-old Romanov became tsar. He grew up to be Peter the Great, and great was literal.
Peter stood over two meters tall. Most of his subjects had to look way up.
He thought Russia was behind Western Europe. So in 1697 he toured Europe, traveling under a fake name, Peter Mikhailov.
In the Netherlands, the tsar of Russia worked in a shipyard as a carpenter. The disguise fooled nobody. He was six foot eight.
Back home, he wanted Russians to look European. And that meant shaving off those long beards.
Your Majesty! My beard is sacred!
Then you can pay for it.
That part's real. Peter taxed beards. Rich merchants paid up to a hundred rubles a year, and one later token said: the beard is a superfluous burden.
He fought Sweden for land on the Baltic Sea. There, on swampy ground by the Neva River, he founded a new capital in 1703: Saint Petersburg.
Forced laborers built the city, and thousands of them died doing it.
In 1709 he crushed the Swedish army at the Battle of Poltava, and Russia became a major European power.
In 1721 he declared Russia an empire, with himself as emperor.
Russia's most famous empress wasn't Russian. She was born Sophie, a German princess, in 1729.
She married the heir to the Russian throne, learned Russian, and took a new name: Catherine.
In 1762 he became Tsar Peter the Third, and made enemies fast. Within six months, Catherine seized the throne with help from the palace guards.
Days later, Peter died in custody, and Catherine ruled alone for thirty-four years.
She wrote letters to famous thinkers like Voltaire, and pushed Russia's borders south to the Black Sea.
Legend says her powerful adviser, Grigory Potemkin, built fake villages to impress her on a tour in 1787. Historians say that's mostly a myth.
In 1812, Napoleon, the French emperor, invaded and reached Moscow. But the city burned, winter came, and most of his huge army never made it home.
Most Russians were still serfs, peasants who belonged to landowners and could even be bought and sold. In 1861, Tsar Alexander the Second freed them.
That's about a third of the whole empire.

show.label: Serfs freed in 1861
show.sub: roughly a third of the empire's people

beats.say: Six years later, Russia sold Alaska to the United States for seven point two million dollars. That's about two cents an acre.

tag.text: William Seward, U.S. Secretary of State

beats.say: In 1914, Tsar Nicholas the Second led Russia into World War One. Millions of Russian soldiers were killed or wounded.
Food ran short. In early 1917, protests in the capital forced Nicholas to give up the throne. Three hundred years of Romanovs, gone.
That autumn, Vladimir Lenin and his Bolsheviks, a radical communist party, seized power. That was the October Revolution.
Fun fact: by our calendar it happened on November 7th. Russia still used an old calendar that ran thirteen days behind.

show.label: The October Revolution, on Russia's old calendar

beats.say: A brutal civil war followed. In 1918, the Bolsheviks executed Nicholas and his whole family.
In 1922 the winners created the Soviet Union, a communist state with Russia at its heart.
After Lenin died in 1924, Joseph Stalin pushed his rivals aside and took control. He forced farmers onto giant state farms and built factories at a furious pace.
The human cost was enormous. A famine in 1932 and 1933 killed millions. Then, in the Great Terror of 1937 and 1938, Stalin's secret police shot around seven hundred thousand people.
In 1941, Nazi Germany invaded. The Battle of Stalingrad, which ended in early 1943, turned the war around.
The Soviets pushed the Germans all the way back, and in spring 1945 their soldiers raised the red flag over Berlin.
But the price was staggering.

show.label: Soviet deaths in World War II

beats.say: After the war, the Soviet Union and the United States became rivals in the Cold War, a standoff where they never fought each other directly.
In 1957 the Soviets launched Sputnik, the first satellite. It was a metal ball about the size of a beach ball, and all it did was beep.
Americans panicked. Then, as you saw, Gagarin flew into space in 1961.
The same year the Soviets tested the Tsar Bomba, the most powerful bomb ever exploded: over three thousand times stronger than the Hiroshima bomb. Its mushroom cloud rose about sixty kilometers high.
In 1962 the Soviets put nuclear missiles in Cuba. For thirteen tense days the world held its breath, then both sides backed down.
By the 1980s, the Soviet economy was struggling. A new leader, Mikhail Gorbachev, tried to open up and reform the system.
Instead, the fifteen Soviet republics, the member states of the union, started breaking away one after another.
On Christmas Day 1991, Gorbachev resigned and the red flag came down over the Kremlin. The next day the Soviet Union was gone, split into fifteen countries.
So that's Russia: Vikings, Mongols, tsars, a revolution and a rocket, in about eleven hundred years.
Next up: the craziest things Napoleon did. See you there.
